title: Valence, Anomalous Behaviour and Chemical Reactivity

pages.title: Use a table position to predict chemistry

blocks.text: Sodium and chlorine sit in the same period but behave very differently. Their outer-shell electron patterns suggest different ways to reach stable arrangements: electron loss, gain or sharing.
Valence and reactivity connect periodic structure with chemical change. The aim is a reasoned prediction, not a claim that all members of a group behave identically.

pages.transition: Relate common combining capacities to the number of outer electrons.

pages.title: Connect main-group valence with outer electrons

blocks.text: For simple main-group compounds, valence often rises from 1 to 4 across a period and then falls towards 0. Elements with one, two or three outer electrons frequently show corresponding valencies; those with five, six or seven often show 8 minus that count.
This introductory rule predicts common combining capacities. It is not a universal formula for every oxidation state, especially in heavier or transition elements.

Combining capacity and ionic charge are related in many simple examples but not identical concepts. In a neutral covalent molecule, atoms share electron pairs; the formula need not imply free ions. Always identify which bonding model the example uses.

pages.transition: Charge neutrality turns simple ion predictions into formulas.

pages.title: Explain familiar formulas using the pattern

blocks.text: Sodium tends to lose one electron to form Na⁺; magnesium often forms Mg²⁺. Chlorine tends to gain one to form Cl⁻. Charge balance therefore gives NaCl and MgCl₂.
The subscripts express the ratio needed for neutrality. MgCl₂ contains one Mg²⁺ per two Cl⁻, not a magnesium ion with a fractional charge.

pages.transition: The smallest members of groups need separate attention.

pages.title: Recognise anomalous second-period behaviour

blocks.text: The first member of a group can differ noticeably from heavier members. Small size, high charge density and distinctive orbital availability make the second-period elements particularly unusual.
The textbook relates this to their compact valence shells and absence of valence d orbitals. Do not mechanically transfer every heavier-element compound or coordination pattern to the first member.

pages.transition: Some competing trends produce similarities along a diagonal.

pages.title: Understand diagonal relationships

blocks.text: Some second-period elements resemble the third-period element diagonally to the right. Lithium–magnesium and beryllium–aluminium are standard examples. Competing trends can produce comparable size-to-charge characteristics.
A diagonal relationship means selected similarities, not that the elements share a group or identical chemistry. Compare the actual property or compound before claiming the resemblance.

pages.transition: Use electron-removal ease to explain a metallic-family trend.

pages.title: Explain metallic reactivity down a group

blocks.text: For alkali metals, larger size and greater shielding down the group generally make the valence electron easier to remove. Metallic reactivity therefore tends to increase down the group.
The trend refers to a particular family and type of reaction. Rate also depends on conditions and physical factors; a periodic argument is not a complete kinetic prediction.

pages.transition: Compare that with an electron-accepting non-metal family.

pages.title: Explain non-metal reactivity qualitatively

blocks.text: Halogens react strongly by accepting electron density or forming bonds. Their ability to act as oxidising agents generally decreases down the group as attraction for electrons becomes less effective.
Do not describe this by reversing only one isolated gas-phase enthalpy trend. Real chemical reactivity involves the full reaction energy balance, including bonds and the surrounding medium.

pages.transition: Oxides provide a useful chemical test of changing character.

pages.title: Relate oxide character to periodic position

blocks.text: Across a main-group period, oxides tend to change from basic through amphoteric to acidic. Basic oxides react with acids; acidic oxides react with bases; amphoteric oxides can react with both.
Na₂O and MgO illustrate basic character, Al₂O₃ amphoteric character, and oxides of later non-metals acidic character. This provides a chemical application of changing metallic character.

An oxide reacts with both hydrochloric acid and a strong base. That observation supports amphoteric character. Its classification comes from two kinds of chemical behaviour, not from merely placing the element halfway across a drawn row.

pages.transition: Work through one complete electronic and charge-balance prediction.

pages.title: Test a prediction against actual structure

blocks.text: Teacher application: compare period 3 sodium and chlorine. Sodium’s 3s¹ configuration favours loss of its single outer electron; chlorine’s 3s²3p⁵ needs one electron to complete its valence shell.
Their combination gives Na⁺ and Cl⁻ in an ionic solid. The periodic pattern predicts useful behaviour, while the completed reaction must still conserve atoms and overall charge.

pages.transition: State the limits of each trend before using it for an unfamiliar reaction.

blocks.text: Valence patterns, group trends and oxide character translate periodic structure into chemistry. Anomalous first members and diagonal relationships remind us that similarities are selective.
State the family, property and conditions when predicting reactivity. Use outer-electron structure and size to explain the trend rather than assuming one rule covers all reactions.

questions.question: Why is MgCl₂ electrically neutral?
questions.answer: One Mg²⁺ balances two Cl⁻, giving total charge zero.

questions.question: Predict a common valency for a group 16 main-group element.
questions.answer: The simple octet pattern suggests 8−6=2, while other oxidation states may occur.

questions.question: Why can the first member of a group be unusual?
questions.answer: Its small size, high charge density and compact valence-orbital set differ from heavier members.

questions.question: Does a diagonal relationship mean identical chemistry?
questions.answer: No. It refers to selected similarities, such as those between Li and Mg.

questions.question: Why does alkali-metal reactivity generally increase down the group?
questions.answer: The outer electron becomes easier to remove as size and shielding increase.

questions.question: What does amphoteric mean for an oxide?
questions.answer: It can react with both acids and bases; Al₂O₃ is a familiar example.

questions.question: Why should reactivity not be inferred from one gas-phase step alone?
questions.answer: The complete reaction involves multiple bond and energy changes, often including solvent effects.
